intro: “Would like” is the polite way to say what you want: “I'd like a coffee, please.” We also use it to offer and invite: “Would you like some tea?” You need it in restaurants, in shops and at work.
objectifs: Use would like + noun and would like + to + verb, with the short form I'd like.
Make a polite request instead of “I want”.
Offer and invite with Would you like…? and answer (Yes, please / I'd love to).
Know the difference between “like” (enjoy in general) and “would like” (want now).

texte: “Would like” is the same for every subject: I would like, she would like, they would like. No s on “like”! In speech, we almost always use the short form: I'd like, you'd like, she'd like, we'd like.
You can put a noun after it: “I'd like a sandwich.” For a verb, you need “to”: “I'd like to go home.”
Question: “Would you like…?” Short answers: “Yes, please.” / “No, thank you.” (for an offer) or “Yes, I would.” / “No, I wouldn't.”

lignes: I'd like a glass of water.
She'd like to study in Canada.
What would you like to drink?
Would you like tea? — Yes, please.

sections.note: The negative “I wouldn't like…” exists but is not common for saying no. To say no politely, say “No, thank you” or “I'd rather not”.

texte: “I want…” is correct, but it can sound direct, even rude, with a waiter, a shop assistant or a stranger. “I'd like…” is the normal polite form.
We often add “please”: “I'd like a ticket to Ghent, please.” In restaurants, you also hear “Can I have…?”, “Could I have…?” and “I'll have…”.
exemples: I'd like a return ticket to Lyon, please.
We'd like to book a table for four.
On the phone to a restaurant.
Could I have the bill, please?
At the end of a meal (US: the check).

texte: “Would you like + noun?” offers something: “Would you like a biscuit?”. “Would you like to + verb?” invites someone: “Would you like to come to my party?”
To accept an invitation: “Yes, I'd love to!” (keep “to” at the end, but don't repeat the verb). To say no politely: “I'd love to, but I can't. I'm busy on Saturday.”
To accept an offer: “Yes, please.”; to say no: “No, thank you.” / “No, thanks.” Don't answer “Yes, I like”!
exemples: Would you like some more rice? — No, thank you. I'm full.
Would you like to have dinner with us on Friday? — I'd love to!
Would you like to come to the cinema? — I'd love to, but I'm working.

texte: “Like” (lesson 33) is about general, permanent tastes: “I like coffee” (I enjoy it). “Would like” is about a wish now: “I'd like a coffee” (I want one now).
The questions are very different: “Do you like tea?” asks about your taste; “Would you like a tea?” is an offer.

lignes: I'd like to dance with you.
Do you like coffee? — Yes, I do.
Would you like a coffee? — Yes, please.
She'd like to travel to Japan.

texte: To say what you want another person to do, use “would like + person + to + verb”. Never use “that” here.
This is very useful at work and to introduce people.
exemples: I'd like you to meet my colleague, Ana.
We'd like you to check this document.

formule: I'd like + noun · I'd like to + verb · Would you like…? — Yes, please. / I'd love to!
prononciation: “would” is /wʊd/: don't say the l. “Would” and “wood” sound the same.
In “I'd like”, you hardly hear the d: /aɪd ˈlaɪk/. Listen carefully: “I like” and “I'd like” sound very similar.
“to” is weak in “I'd like to go” /tə/, but strong at the end of a sentence: “I'd love to!” /tuː/.
An offer goes up at the end: “Would you like some TEA? ↗”.
erreurs: I want a coffee. (to a waiter)
I'd like a coffee, please.
“I want” can sound rude; “I'd like” is polite.
I would like go to Paris.
I would like to go to Paris.
Would like + to + verb.
Do you like a coffee? (an offer)
Would you like a coffee?
To offer: “Would you like…?”.
Would you like some tea? — Yes, I like.
Would you like some tea? — Yes, please.
To accept an offer: Yes, please.
I'd like going to the beach.
I'd like to go to the beach.
After would like: to + verb, not -ing.
She'd likes a new phone.
She'd like a new phone.
No s after “would”.
Would you like to come? — Yes, I'd love.
Would you like to come? — Yes, I'd love to.
Keep “to” at the end.
I would like that you come.
I'd like you to come.
would like + person + to + verb, never “that”.

dialogue.contexte: In a beach restaurant in Kribi, Cameroon. Nadia and her Belgian colleague Pieter order food.
lignes: Good evening. Would you like something to drink?
Yes, please. I'd like a fresh pineapple juice.
And I'd like a bottle of water, please.
Of course. And what would you like to eat?
I'd like the grilled fish with plantain.
The same for me. I'd like to try the local food.
Would you like some chilli sauce?
Yes, please, but just a little!
Pieter, would you like to visit the waterfalls tomorrow?

exercices.consigne: Complete with like, likes or 'd like.
items: I ___ a cup of tea, please.
I ___ tea. I drink it every morning.
She ___ dancing. She goes every Saturday.
We ___ to book a table for two.

exercices.consigne: Make the request more polite with I'd like or Would you like.
items: I want a glass of water.
I'd like a glass of water, please.
Do you want to come with us?
Would you like to come with us?

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: I'd like have a tea, please.
I'd like a tea, please. / I'd like to have a cup of tea, please.
Would you like some cake? — Yes, I like.
Would you like some cake? — Yes, please.
She'd like to study in Montreal.
Would you like to come to my party? — I'd love!
Would you like to come to my party? — I'd love to!
I'd like that you meet my brother.
I'd like you to meet my brother.

exercices.consigne: You are in a restaurant. Write your order (drink, main course, dessert) in three sentences with I'd like, then invite a friend to do something this weekend with Would you like to…?
items: I'd like a glass of orange juice, please. For my main course, I'd like the chicken with rice. And I'd like a chocolate cake for dessert. Would you like to go to the beach with me on Saturday?

a_retenir: I'd like + noun (I'd like a coffee); I'd like + to + verb (I'd like to go). No s, no -ing.
“I'd like” is more polite than “I want”.
Offer: Would you like…? — Yes, please. / No, thank you.
Invitation: Would you like to…? — I'd love to! / I'd love to, but I can't.
like = enjoy (in general); would like = want (now). I'd like you to meet… (no “that”).
